</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S6" title="6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> includes several application examples showing how recurrent models naturally simplify LLM usecases.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S7" title="7 What Mechanisms Emerge at Scale in Recurrent-Depth Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> visualizes what computation patterns emerge at scale with this architecture and training objective, showing that context-dependent behaviors emerge in latent space, such as “orbiting” when responding to prompts requiring numerical reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/arch.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:538/143;" width="538" height="143"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>A visualization of the Architecture, as described in <a href="#S3" title="3 A scalable recurrent architecture" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Each block consists of a number of sub-layers. The blue prelude block embeds the inputs into latent space, where the green shared <span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">recurrent block</span> is a block of layers that is repeated to compute the final latent state, which is decoded by the layers of the red coda block.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>A scalable recurrent architecture</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section we will describe our proposed architecture for a transformer with latent recurrent depth, discussing design choices and small-scale ablations. A diagram of the architecture can be found in <a href="#S2.F2" title="In ———————— Table of Contents ———————— ‣ 2 Why Train Models with Recurrent Depth?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We always refer to the sequence dimension as <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, the hidden dimension of the model as <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, and its vocabulary as the set <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Macroscopic Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model is primarily structured around decoder-only transformer blocks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib161" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib124" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. However these blocks are structured into three functional groups, the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">prelude</span> <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>, which embeds the input data into a latent space using multiple transformer layers, then the core <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">recurrent block</span> <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>, which is the central unit of recurrent computation modifying states <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times h}</annotation></semantics></math>, and finally the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">coda</span> <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, which un-embeds from latent space using several layers and also contains the prediction head of the model. The core block is set between the prelude and coda blocks, and by looping the core we can put an indefinite amount of verses in our song.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given a number of recurrent iterations <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, and a sequence of input tokens <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in V^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in V^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> these groups are used in the following way to produce output probabilities <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times|V|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐩</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times|V|}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=P(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=P(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}I_{n\cdot h})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}I_{n\cdot h})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle=R(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})\qquad\textnormal{for}\quad i\in\{1,\dots,r\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mtext>for</mtext><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=R(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})\qquad\textnormal{for}\quad i\in\{1,\dots,r\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{p}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=C(\mathbf{s}_{r})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=C(\mathbf{s}_{r}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is some standard deviation for initializing the random state. This process is shown in <a href="#S2.F2" title="In ———————— Table of Contents ———————— ‣ 2 Why Train Models with Recurrent Depth?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Given an init random state <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model repeatedly applies the core block <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>, which accepts the latent state <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and the embedded input <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> and outputs a new latent state <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. After finishing all iterations, the coda block processes the last state and produces the probabilities of the next token.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This architecture is based on deep thinking literature, where it is shown that injecting the latent inputs <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> in every step <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and initializing the latent vector with a random state stabilizes the recurrence and promotes convergence to a steady state independent of initialization, i.e. <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">path independence</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anil et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Motivation for this Design.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This recurrent design is the minimal setup required to learn stable iterative operators.
A good example is gradient descent of a function <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐲</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> may be the variable of interest and <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math> the data. Gradient descent on this function starts from an initial random state, here <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, and repeatedly applies a simple operation (the gradient of the function it optimizes), that depends on the previous state <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{k}</annotation></semantics></math> and data <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that we need to use <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}</annotation></semantics></math> in every step to actually optimize our function. Similarly we repeatedly inject the data <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> in our set-up in every step of the recurrence. If <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> was provided only at the start, e.g. via <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{0}=\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{0}=\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, then the iterative process would not be stable<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Stable in the sense that <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> cannot be a monotone operator if it does not depend on <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, and so cannot represent gradient descent on strictly convex, data-dependent functions, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bauschke et al., 2011</a>)</cite></span></span></span>, as its solution would depend only on its boundary conditions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The structure of using several layers to embed input tokens into a hidden latent space is based on empirical results analyzing standard fixed-depth transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib143" title="" class="ltx_ref">Skean et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib149" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This body of research shows that the initial and the end layers of LLMs are noticeably different, whereas middle layers are interchangeable and permutable. For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al. (2024)</a></cite> show that within a few layers standard models already embed sub-word tokens into single concepts in latent space, on which the model then operates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Remark 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> </span>(Is this a Diffusion Model?)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This iterative architecture will look familiar to the other modern iterative modeling paradigm, diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib146" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song and Ermon, 2019</a>)</cite>, especially latent diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib127" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. We ran several ablations with iterative schemes even more similar to diffusion models, such as <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i}=R(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})+\mathbf{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐧</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i}=R(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})+\mathbf{n}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{i}I_{n\cdot h})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐧</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{i}I_{n\cdot h})</annotation></semantics></math>, but find the injection of noise not to help in our preliminary experiments, which is possibly connected to our training objective. We also evaluated and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i}=R_{i}(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i}=R_{i}(\mathbf{e},\mathbf{s}_{i-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. a core block that takes the current step as input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib123" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles and Xie, 2023</a>)</cite>, but find that this interacts badly with path independence, leading to models that cannot extrapolate.</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Microscopic Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Within each group, we broadly follow standard transformer layer design. Each block contains multiple layers, and each layer contains a standard, causal self-attention block using RoPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib147" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2021</a>)</cite> with a base of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50000</annotation></semantics></math>, and a gated SiLU MLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer, 2020</a>)</cite>. We use RMSNorm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib181" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang and Sennrich, 2019</a>)</cite> as our normalization function. The model has learnable biases on queries and keys, and nowhere else. To stabilize the recurrence, we order all layers in the following “sandwich” format, using norm layers <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is related, but not identical to similar strategies in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib156" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team Gemma et al., 2024</a>)</cite>:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle n_{2}\left(\mathbf{x}_{l-1}+\textnormal{Attn}(n_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{l-1}))\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>Attn</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle n_{2}\left(\mathbf{x}_{l-1}+\textnormal{Attn}(n_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{l-1}))\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{l}=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{l}=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle n_{4}\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}+\textnormal{MLP}(n_{3}(\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}))\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext>MLP</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle n_{4}\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}+\textnormal{MLP}(n_{3}(\hat{\mathbf{x}_{l}}))\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">While at small scales, most normalization strategies, e.g. pre-norm, post-norm and others, work almost equally well, we ablate these options and find that this normalization is required to train the recurrence at scale<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Note also that technically <math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is superfluous, but we report here the exact norm setup with which we trained the final model.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given an embedding matrix <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> and embedding scale <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, the prelude block first embeds input tokens <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma E(\mathbf{x})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma E(\mathbf{x})</annotation></semantics></math>, and then to applies <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{P}</annotation></semantics></math> many prelude layers with the layout described above.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our core recurrent block <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> starts with an adapter matrix <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A:\mathbb{R}^{2h}\to\mathbb{R}^{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>h</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A:\mathbb{R}^{2h}\to\mathbb{R}^{h}</annotation></semantics></math> mapping the concatenation of <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> into the hidden dimension <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. While re-incorporation of initial embedding features via addition rather than concatenation works equally well for smaller models, we find that concatenation works best at scale.
This is then fed into <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{R}</annotation></semantics></math> transformer layers. At the end of the core block the output is again rescaled with an RMSNorm <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The coda contains <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> layers, normalization by <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{c}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{c}</annotation></semantics></math>, and projection into the vocabulary using tied embeddings <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>E</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, we can summarize the architecture by the triplet <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(l_{P},l_{R},l_{C})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(l_{P},l_{R},l_{C})</annotation></semantics></math>, describing the number of layers in each stage, and by the number of recurrences <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, which may vary in each forward pass. We train a number of small-scale models with shape <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1,4,1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1,4,1)</annotation></semantics></math> and hidden size <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=1024" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=1024</annotation></semantics></math>, in addition to a large model with shape <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2,4,2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2,4,2)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=5280" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5280</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=5280</annotation></semantics></math>. This model has only <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> “real” layers, but when the recurrent block is iterated, e.g. 32 times, it unfolds to an effective depth of <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2+4r+2=132" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>132</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2+4r+2=132</annotation></semantics></math> layers, constructing computation chains that can be deeper than even the largest fixed-depth transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib92" title="" class="ltx_ref">Levine et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib110" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Training Objective</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Recurrent Models through Unrolling.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure that the model can function when we scale up recurrent iterations at test-time, we randomly sample iteration counts during training, assigning a random number of iterations <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> to every input sequence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib135" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al., 2021b</a>)</cite>. We optimize the expectation of the loss function <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> over random samples <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> from distribution <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and random iteration counts <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> from distribution <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\in X}\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\Lambda}L\left(m_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},r),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>∼</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\in X}\mathbb{E}_{r\sim\Lambda}L\left(m_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},r),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> represents the model output, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> shifted left, i.e., the next tokens in the sequence <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We choose <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math> to be a <span id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">log-normal Poisson distribution</span>. Given a targeted mean recurrence <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{r}+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{r}+1</annotation></semantics></math> and a variance that we set to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma=\frac{1}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma=\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can sample from this distribution via</p>
<table id="S3.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\tau</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\log(\bar{r})-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2},\sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}(\log(\bar{r})-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{2},\sigma)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle r</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{P}(e^{\tau})+1," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>τ</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sim\mathcal{P}(e^{\tau})+1,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">given the normal distribution <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}</annotation></semantics></math> and Poisson distribution <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math>, see <a href="#S3.F3" title="In Training Recurrent Models through Unrolling. ‣ 3.3 Training Objective ‣ 3 A scalable recurrent architecture" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The distribution most often samples values less than <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{r}</annotation></semantics></math>, but it contains a heavy tail of occasional events in which significantly more iterations are taken.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/log-normal-poisson-dist.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:538/364;" width="538" height="364"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>We use a log-normal Poisson Distribution to sample the number of recurrent iterations for each training step.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Truncated Backpropagation.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To keep computation and memory low at train time, we backpropagate through only the last <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> iterations of the recurrent unit. This enables us to train with the heavy-tailed Poisson distribution <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, as maximum activation memory and backward compute is now independent of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>. We fix <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=8</annotation></semantics></math> in our main experiments. At small scale, this works as well as sampling <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> uniformly, but with set fixed, the overall memory usage in each step of training is equal. Note that the prelude block still receives gradient updates in every step, as its output <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math> is injected in every step. This setup resembles truncated backpropagation through time, as commonly done with RNNs, although our setup is recurrent in depth rather than time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib165" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams and Peng, 1990</a>; <a href="#bib.bib112" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al., 2011</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Training a large-scale recurrent-depth Language Model</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After verifying that we can reliably train small test models up to 10B tokens, we move on to larger-scale runs. Given our limited compute budget, we could either train multiple tiny models too small to show emergent effects or scaling, or train a single medium-scale model. Based on this, we prepared for a single run, which we detail below.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Training Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe the training setup, separated into architecture, optimization setup and pretraining data.
We publicly release all training data, pretraining code, and a selection of intermediate model checkpoints.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pretraining Data.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given access to only enough compute for a single large scale model run, we opted for a dataset mixture that maximized the potential for emergent reasoning behaviors, not necessarily for optimal benchmark performance. Our final mixture is heavily skewed towards code and mathematical reasoning data with (hopefully) just enough general webtext to allow the model to acquire standard language modeling abilities. All sources are publicly available. We provide an overview in <a href="#S4.F4" title="In Tokenization and Packing Details. ‣ 4.1 Training Setup ‣ 4 Training a large-scale recurrent-depth Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Allen-Zhu and Li (2024)</a></cite>, we directly mix relevant instruction data into the pretraining data. However, due to compute and time constraints, we were not able to ablate this mixture. We expect that a more careful data preparation could further improve the model’s performance. We list all data sources in <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Pretraining Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Tokenization and Packing Details.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct a vocabulary of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="65536" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>65536</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">65536</annotation></semantics></math> tokens via BPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib137" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sennrich et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, using the implementation of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan (2024)</a></cite>. In comparison to conventional tokenizer training, we construct our tokenizer directly on the instruction data split of our pretraining corpus, to maximize tokenization efficiency on the target domain. We also substantially modify the pre-tokenization regex (e.g. of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dagan et al. (2024)</a></cite>) to better support code, contractions and LaTeX. We include a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;|begin_text|&gt;</span> token at the start of every document. After tokenizing our pretraining corpus, we pack our tokenized documents into sequences of length 4096. When packing, we discard document ends that would otherwise lack previous context, to fix an issue described as the “grounding problem” in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ding et al. (2024)</a></cite>, aside from several long-document sources of mathematical content, which we preserve in their entirety.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/data_pie_chart.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/391;" width="673" height="391"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Distribution of data sources that are included during training. The majority of our data is comprised of generic web-text, scientific writing and code.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture and Initialization.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We scale the architecture described in <a href="#S3" title="3 A scalable recurrent architecture" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, setting the layers to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(2,4,2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2,4,2)</annotation></semantics></math>, and train with a mean recurrence value of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{r}=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{r}=32</annotation></semantics></math>. We mainly scale by increasing the hidden size to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=5280" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5280</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=5280</annotation></semantics></math>, which yields <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="55" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>55</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">55</annotation></semantics></math> heads of size of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="96" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>96</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">96</annotation></semantics></math>. The MLP inner dimension is <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17920" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>17920</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17920</annotation></semantics></math> and the RMSNorm <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>. Overall this model shape has about <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters in non-recurrent prelude and head, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5</annotation></semantics></math>B parameters in the core recurrent block, and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math>B in the tied input embedding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At small scales, most sensible initialization schemes work. However, at larger scales, we use the initialization of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib154" title="" class="ltx_ref">Takase et al. (2024)</a></cite> which prescribes a variance of <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{h}^{2}=\frac{2}{5h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{h}^{2}=\frac{2}{5h}</annotation></semantics></math>. We initialize all parameters from a truncated normal distribution (truncated at <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>) with this variance, except all out-projection layers, where the variance is set to <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\textnormal{out}}^{2}=\frac{1}{5hl}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mtext>out</mtext><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\textnormal{out}}^{2}=\frac{1}{5hl}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=l_{P}+\bar{r}l_{R}+l_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>R</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=l_{P}+\bar{r}l_{R}+l_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> the number of effective layers, which is 132 for this model. As a result, the out-projection layers are initialized with fairly small values <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goyal et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. The output of the embedding layer is scaled by <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sqrt{h}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msqrt><mi>h</mi></msqrt><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{h}</annotation></semantics></math>. To match this initialization, the state <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is also sampled from a truncated normal distribution, here with variance <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{s}^{2}=\frac{2}{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>5</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{s}^{2}=\frac{2}{5}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Locked-Step Sampling.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enable synchronization between parallel workers, we sample a single depth <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> for each micro-batch of training, which we synchronize across workers (otherwise workers would idle while waiting for the model with the largest <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> to complete its backward pass). We verify at small scale that this modification improves compute utilization without impacting convergence speed, but note that at large batch sizes, training could be further improved by optimally sampling and scheduling independent steps <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> on each worker, to more faithfully model the expectation over steps in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training Recurrent Models through Unrolling. ‣ 3.3 Training Objective ‣ 3 A scalable recurrent architecture" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Optimizer and Learning Rate Schedule.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train using the Adam optimizer with decoupled weight regularization (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{1}=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{1}=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{2}=0.95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{2}=0.95</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=$5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}$" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>×</mtext><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=$5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}$</annotation></semantics></math>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017</a>)</cite>, modified to include update clipping <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib167" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> and removal of the <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> constant as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Everett et al. (2024)</a></cite>. We clip gradients above <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>. We train with warm-up and a constant learning rate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib180" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping and Goldstein, 2023</a>)</cite>, warming up to our maximal learning rate within the first <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4096</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4096</annotation></semantics></math> steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Compute Setup and Hardware</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train this model using compute time allocated on the Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Frontier</span> supercomputer. This HPE Cray system contains 9408 compute nodes with AMD MI250X GPUs, connected via 4xHPE Slingshot-11 NICs. The scheduling system is orchestrated through SLURM. We train in bfloat16 mixed precision using a PyTorch-based implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib177" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zamirai et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/token_corr.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/179;" width="673" height="179"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Plots of the initial 10000 steps for the first two failed attempts and the final, successful run (“Main”). Note the hidden state collapse (middle) and collapse of the recurrence (right) in the first two failed runs, underlining the importance of our architecture and initialization in inducing a recurrent model and explain the underperformance of these runs in terms of pretraining loss (left).</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Device Speed and Parallelization Strategy.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Nominally, each MI250X chip<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              Technically, each node contains 4 dual-chip MI250X cards, but its main software stack (ROCm runtime) treats these chips as fully independent.</span></span></span> achieves 192 TFLOP per GPU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">AMD, 2021</a>)</cite>. For a single matrix multiplication, we measure a maximum achievable speed on these GPUs of 125 TFLOP/s on our software stack (ROCM 6.2.0, PyTorch 2.6 pre-release 11/02) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bekman, 2023</a>)</cite>. Our implementation, using extensive PyTorch compilation and optimization of the hidden dimension to <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h=5280" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5280</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h=5280</annotation></semantics></math> achieves a single-node training speed of 108.75 TFLOP/s, i.e. 87% AFU (“Achievable Flop Utilization”). Due to the weight sharing inherent in our recurrent design, even our largest model is still small enough to be trained using only data (not tensor) parallelism, with only optimizer sharding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib126" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rajbhandari et al., 2020</a>)</cite> and gradient checkpointing on a per-iteration granularity. With a batch size of 1 per GPU we end up with a global batch size of 16M tokens per step, minimizing inter-GPU communication bandwidth.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When we run at scale on 4096 GPUs, we achieve 52-64 TFLOP/s per GPU, i.e. 41%-51% AFU, or 1-1.2M tokens per second. To achieve this, we wrote a hand-crafted distributed data parallel implementation to circumvent a critical AMD interconnect issue, which we describe in more detail in <a href="#Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" title="RCCL Interconnect Handling ‣ A.2 Implementation Details ‣ Potential Implications of This Work" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>. Overall, we believe this may be the largest language model training run to completion in terms of number of devices used in parallel on an AMD cluster, as of time of writing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training Timeline.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training proceeded through 21 segments of up to 12 hours, which scheduled on Frontier mostly in early December 2024. We also ran a baseline comparison, where we train the same architecture but in a feedforward manner with only 1 pass through the core/recurrent block. This trained with the same setup for 180B tokens on 256 nodes with a batch size of 2 per GPU. Ultimately, we were able to schedule 795B tokens of pretraining of the main model. Due to our constant learning rate schedule, we were able to add additional segments “on-demand”, when an allocation happened to be available.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<td id="S4.T1.2.14.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">57.77</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T1.2.15" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T1.2.15.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r">Ours, (<math id="S4.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=32</annotation></semantics></math>)</th>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">3.5B</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r">0.8T</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">69.91</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">38.23</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">65.21</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">31.38</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.15.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">38.80</td>
