<td id="S4.T1.2.15.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">59.43</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Importance of Norms and Initializations at Scale</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At small scales all normalization strategies worked, and we observed only tiny differences between initializations. The same was not true at scale. The first training run we started was set up with the same block sandwich structure as described above, but parameter-free RMSNorm layers, no embedding scale <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, a parameter-free adapter <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{e})=\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐞</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>𝐞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{e})=\mathbf{s}+\mathbf{e}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a peak learning rate of <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3.m1" class="ltx_markedasmath" alttext="4\text{\times}{10}^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mtext>×</mtext><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\text{\times}{10}^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>. As shown in <a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.2 Compute Setup and Hardware ‣ 4 Training a large-scale recurrent-depth Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, this run (“Bad Run 1”, orange), quickly stalled.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the run obviously stopped improving in training loss (left plot), we find that this stall is due to the model’s representation collapsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib119" title="" class="ltx_ref">Noci et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. The correlation of hidden states in the token dimension quickly goes to 1.0 (middle plot), meaning the model predicts the same hidden state for every token in the sequence.
We find that this is an initialization issue that arises due to the recurrence operation. Every iteration of the recurrence block increases token correlation, mixing the sequence until collapse.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We attempt to fix this by introducing the embedding scale factor, switching back to a conventional pre-normalization block, and switching to the learned adapter. Initially, these changes appear to remedy the issue. Even though token correlation shoots close to 1.0 at the start (“Bad Run 2”, green), the model recovers after the first 150 steps. However, we quickly find that this training run is not able to leverage test-time compute effectively (right plot), as validation perplexity is the same whether 1 or 32 recurrences are used. This initialization and norm setup has led to a local minimum as the model has learned early to ignore the incoming state <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}</annotation></semantics></math>, preventing further improvements.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In a third, and final run (“Main”, blue), we fix this issue by reverting back to the sandwich block format, and further dropping the peak learning rate to <math id="S4.SS3.p4.m1.m1" class="ltx_markedasmath" alttext="4\text{\times}{10}^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mtext>×</mtext><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\text{\times}{10}^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>. This run starts smoothly, never reaches a token correlation close to 1.0, and quickly overtakes the previous run by utilizing the recurrence and improving with more iterations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">With our successful configuration, training continues smoothly for the next 750B tokens without notable interruptions or loss spikes. We plot training loss and perplexity at different recurrence steps in <a href="#S4.F6" title="In Training Timeline. ‣ 4.2 Compute Setup and Hardware ‣ 4 Training a large-scale recurrent-depth Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. In our material, we refer to the final checkpoint of this run as our “main model”, which we denote as <span id="S4.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Huginn-0125<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">4</span></span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <span id="footnote4.10" class="ltx_ERROR undefined">\textipa</span><span id="footnote4.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">/hu: gIn/, transl. “thought”, is a raven depicted in Norse mythology. Corvids are surprisingly intelligent for their size, and and of course, as birds, able to unfold their wings at test-time.</span></span></span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Benchmark Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train our final model for 800B tokens, and a non-recurrent baseline for 180B tokens. We evaluate these checkpoints against other open-source models trained on fully public datasets (like ours) of a similar size. We compare against Amber <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023c</a>)</cite>, Pythia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and a number of OLMo 1&amp;2 variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Groeneveld et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">AI2, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib157" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team OLMo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. We execute all standard benchmarks through the lm-eval harness <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and code benchmarks via bigcode-bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib187" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuo et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Standard Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, it is not straightforward to place our model in direct comparison to other large language models, all of which are small variations of the fixed-depth transformer architecture. While our model has only 3.5B parameters and hence requires only modest interconnect bandwidth during pretraining, it chews through raw FLOPs close to what a 32B parameter transformer would consume during pretraining, and can continuously improve in performance with test-time scaling up to FLOP budgets equivalent to a standard 50B parameter fixed-depth transformer.
It is also important to note a few caveats of the main training run when interpreting the results. First, our main checkpoint is trained for only 47000 steps on a broadly untested mixture, and the learning rate is never cooled down from its peak. As an academic project, the model is trained only on publicly available data and the 800B token count, while large in comparison to older fully open-source models such as the Pythia series, is small in comparison to modern open-source efforts such as OLMo, and tiny in comparison to the datasets used to train industrial open-weight models.</p>
</div>

<figure id="S5.T3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:195.1pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 3: </span>Evaluation on code benchmarks, MBPP and HumanEval. We report pass@1 for both datasets.</figcaption>
<div id="S5.T3.fig2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:185.4pt;height:111.9pt;vertical-align:-54.3pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-48.4pt,29.2pt) scale(0.656947817955638,0.656947817955638) ;">
<table id="S5.T3.fig2.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T3.fig2.1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T3.fig2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">Model</th>

<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Disclaimers aside, we collect results for established benchmark tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib157" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team OLMo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> in <a href="#S4.T1" title="In Training Timeline. ‣ 4.2 Compute Setup and Hardware ‣ 4 Training a large-scale recurrent-depth Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and show all models side-by-side. In direct comparison we see that our model outperforms the older Pythia series and is roughly comparable to the first OLMo generation, OLMo-7B in most metrics, but lags behind the later OLMo models trained larger, more carefully curated datasets. For the first recurrent-depth model for language to be trained at this scale, and considering the limitations of the training run, we find these results promising and certainly suggestive that further research into latent recurrence as an approach to test-time scaling is warranted.</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T4.2.1.6.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">47.10</td>
<td id="S5.T4.2.1.6.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">49.41</td>
<td id="S5.T4.2.1.6.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.00/0.00</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Math and Coding Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate the model on math and coding. For math, we evaluate GSM8k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> (as zero-shot and in the 8-way CoT setup), MATH (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>)</cite> with the Minerva evaluation rules <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib93" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewkowycz et al., 2022</a>)</cite>) and MathQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amini et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. For coding, we check MBPP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Austin et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and HumanEval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Here we find that our model significantly surpasses all models except the latest OLMo-2 model in mathematical reasoning, as measured on GSM8k and MATH.
On coding benchmarks the model beats all other general-purpose open-source models, although it does not outperform dedicated code models, such as StarCoder2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lozhkov et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, trained for several trillion tokens.
We also note that while further improvements in language modeling are slowing down, as expected at this training scale, both code and mathematical reasoning continue to improve steadily throughout training, see <a href="#S5.F8" title="In 5.2 Math and Coding Benchmarks ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/gsm8k_hella_swag_humaneval_tasks_performance_vs_semilogx_recurrence.svg" id="S5.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:505/440;" width="505" height="440"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>Performance on GSM8K CoT (strict match and flexible match), HellaSwag (acc norm.), and HumanEval (pass@1). As we increase compute, the performance on these benchmarks increases. HellaSwag only needs <math id="S5.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8</annotation></semantics></math> recurrences to achieve near peak performance while other benchmarks make use of more compute.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.F8" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/gsm8k_cot_vs_tokens_trained_rec.svg" id="S5.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:216/185;" width="216" height="185"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/hellaswag_vs_tokens_trained_rec.svg" id="S5.F8.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:216/185;" width="216" height="185"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/humaneval_vs_tokens_trained_rec.svg" id="S5.F8.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:216/185;" width="216" height="185"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>GSM8K CoT, HellaSwag, and HumanEval performance over the training tokens with different recurrences at test-time. We evaluate GSM8K CoT with chat template and 8-way few shot as multiturn. HellaSwag and HumanEval are zero-shot with no chat template. Model performance on harder tasks grows almost linearly with the training budget, if provided sufficient
test-time compute.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Where does recurrence help most?</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How much of this performance can we attribute to recurrence, and how much to other factors, such as dataset, tokenization and architectural choices? In <a href="#S5.T4" title="In 5.1 Standard Benchmarks ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we compare our recurrent model against its non-recurrent twin, which we trained to 180B tokens in the exact same setting. In direct comparison of both models at 180B tokens, we see that the recurrent model outperforms its baseline with an especially pronounced advantage on harder tasks, such as the ARC challenge set. On other tasks, such as SciQ, which requires straightforward recall of scientific facts, performance of the models is more similar. We observe that gains through reasoning are especially prominent on GSM8k, where the 180B recurrent model is already 5 times better than the baseline at this early snapshot in the pretraining process.
We also note that the recurrent model, when evaluated with only a single recurrence, effectively stops improving between the early 180B checkpoint and the 800B checkpoint, showing that further improvements are not built into the prelude or coda non-recurrent layers but encoded entirely into the iterations of the recurrent block.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Further, we chart the improvement as a function of test-time compute on several of these tasks for the main model in <a href="#S5.F7" title="In 5.2 Math and Coding Benchmarks ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. We find that saturation is highly task-dependent, on easier tasks the model saturates quicker, whereas it benefits from more compute on others.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/arc_challenge_fit_acc.svg" id="S5.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:337/186;" width="337" height="186"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span>The saturation point in un-normalized accuracy via test-time recurrence on the ARC challenge set is correlated with the number of few-shot examples. The model uses more recurrence to extract more information from the additional few-shot examples, making use of more compute if more context is given.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S5.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Comparison of Open and Closed QA Performance (%) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib111" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mihaylov et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. In the open exam, a relevant fact is provided before the question is asked. In this setting, our smaller model closes the gap to other open-source models, indicating that the model is capable, but has fewer facts memorized.</figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Recurrence and Context</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate ARC-C performance as a function of recurrence and number of few-shot examples in the context in <a href="#S5.F9" title="In 5.3 Where does recurrence help most? ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. Interestingly, without few-shot examples to consider, the model saturates in compute around 8-12 iterations. However, when more context is given, the model can reason about more information in context, which it does, saturating around 20 iterations if 1 example is provided, and 32 iterations, if 25-50 examples are provided, mirroring generalization improvements shown for recurrence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib173" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Similarly, we see that if we re-evaluate OBQA in <a href="#S5.T5" title="In 5.3 Where does recurrence help most? ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, but do not run the benchmark in the default lm-eval "closed-book" format and rather provide a relevant fact, our recurrent model improves significantly almost closing the gap to OLMo-2. Intuitively this makes sense, as the recurrent models has less capacity to memorize facts but more capacity to reason about its context.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Improvements through Weight Averaging</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to our constant learning rate, we can materialize further improvements through weight averaging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izmailov et al., 2018</a>)</cite> to simulate the result of a cooldown <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hägele et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We use an exponential moving average starting from our last checkpoint with <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, incorporating the last 75 checkpoints with a dilation factor of 7, a modification to established protocols <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaddour, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib130" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sanyal et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We provide this EMA model as well, which further improves GMS8k performance to <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="47.23\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>47.23</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">47.23\%</annotation></semantics></math> flexible (<math id="S5.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="38.59\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>38.59</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">38.59\%</annotation></semantics></math> strict), when tested at <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=64</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/main_categories.svg" id="S5.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/183;" width="673" height="183"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Histograms of zero-shot, per-token adaptive exits based on KL difference between steps for questions from MMLU categories, with and without zero-shot continuous CoT. The mean of each distribution is given in the legends. The exit threshold is fixed to <math id="S5.F10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>×</mtext><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>. We see that the model converges quicker on high school mathematics than tasks such as logical fallacies or moral scenarios. On some tasks, such as philosophy, the model is able to effectively re-use states in its latent CoT and converge quickly on a subset of tokens, leading to fewer steps required overall.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from encouraging performance in mathematical and code reasoning, recurrent-depth models turn out to be surprisingly natural tools to support a number of methods that require substantial effort with standard transformers. In the next section, we provide a non-exhaustive overview.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Zero-Shot Adaptive Compute at Test-Time</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have shown that the model is capable of varying compute on a per-query level, running the model in different recurrence modes. This is after all also how the model is trained, as in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training Recurrent Models through Unrolling. ‣ 3.3 Training Objective ‣ 3 A scalable recurrent architecture" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. However, it would be
more efficient in practice to stop recurring early when predictions are easy, and only spend compute on hard decisions. Other work, especially when based on standard transformers, requires models trained specifically for <span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">early exits</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elbayad et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Banino et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, or models finetuned with exit heads on every layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib132" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuster et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
To test our model’s zero-shot exit abilities, we choose a simple exit criterion to evaluate convergence, the KL-divergence between two successive steps. If this divergence falls below <math id="S6.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext>×</mtext><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\text{\times}{10}^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, we stop iterating, sample the output token, and move to generate the next token.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We show this zero-shot per-token adaptive compute behavior in <a href="#S5.F10" title="In 5.4 Improvements through Weight Averaging ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, where we plot the distribution of steps taken before the exit condition is hit. We do this for the first 50 questions from different MMLU categories, asked in free-form chat. Interestingly, the number of steps required to exit differs notably between categories, with the model exiting earlier on high school mathematics, but taking on average 3.5 steps more on moral scenarios.
As a preliminary demonstration, we verify on MTBench that this adaptivity does not significantly impact performance in a conversational benchmark setting (standard: <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.63" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.63</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.63</annotation></semantics></math>, early exits: <math id="S6.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.56" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.56</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.56</annotation></semantics></math> see Appendix <a href="#A0.T6" title="" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S6.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Remark 6.1</span></span><span id="S6.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic"> </span>(What about missing KV-cache entries?)<span id="S6.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">.</span></h6>
<div id="S6.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditionally, a concern with token-wise early exits for models with self-attention is that it breaks KV-caching in a fundamental way. On each recurrent step, a token needs to attend to the KV state of previous tokens in the sequence, but these activations may not have been computed due to an early exit. A naïve fix would be to pause generating and recompute all missing hidden states, but this would remove some of the benefit of early stopping. Instead, as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elbayad et al. (2019)</a></cite>, we attend to the last, deepest available KV states in the cache. Because all recurrent KV cache entries are generated by the same K,V projection matrices from successive hidden states, they “match”, and therefore the model is able to attend to the latest cache entry from every previous token, even if computed at different recurrent depths.</p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Zero-Shot KV-cache Sharing</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A different avenue to increase efficiency is to reduce the memory footprint of the KV-cache by sharing the cache between layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">character.ai, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brandon et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Typically, transformers must be trained from scratch with this capability. However, as discussed in the previous section, we find that we can simply share KV-caches in our model with minimal impact to performance. We set a fixed KV-cache budget for the recurrence at every token <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, and at iteration <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, read and write the cache entry <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\bmod k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>mod</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\bmod k</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, we set a maximum KV-cache budget of 16 steps, overwriting the KV-cache of the 1st step when executing the 17th step, and so forth. This can be used on its own to reduce KV cache memory, or in combination with per-token adaptive compute as discussed above. On MTBench, this does not reduce performance (cache budget of <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5.86" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5.86</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5.86</annotation></semantics></math>, see Appendix <a href="#A0.T6" title="" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F11" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/convergence_chart_range_I_74_103.png" id="S6.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/408;" width="673" height="408" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 11: </span>Convergence of latent states for every token in a sequence (going top to bottom) and latent iterations (going left to right), plotting the distance a final iterate <math id="S6.F11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, which we set with <math id="S6.F11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=128</annotation></semantics></math>. Shown is an unsafe question posed to the model. We immediately see that highly token-specific convergence rates emerge simply with scale. This is interesting, as the model is only trained with <math id="S6.F11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> fixed for whole sequences seen during training. We see that convergence is especially slow on the key part of the question, <span id="S6.F11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">really wrong</span>-ed.We further see that the model also learns different behaviors, we see an oscillating pattern in latent space, here most notably for the <span id="S6.F11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">school</span> token. Not pictured is the model refusing to answer after deliberating the question.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Zero-Shot Continuous Chain-of-Thought</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By attending to the output of later steps of previous tokens in the early steps of current tokens, as described in the KV-cache sharing section, we actually construct a computation that is deeper than the current number of recurrence steps. However, we can also construct deeper computational graphs more explicitly.
Instead of sampling a random initial state <math id="S6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> at every generation step, we can warm-start with the last state <math id="S6.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math> from the previous token. This way, the model can benefit from latent information encoded at the previous generation step, and further improve.
As shown in <a href="#S5.F10" title="In 5.4 Improvements through Weight Averaging ‣ 5 Benchmark Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, this reduces the average number of steps required to converge by 1-2. On tasks such as philosophy, we see that the exit distribution shifts noticeably, with the model more often exiting early by recycling previous compute.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This is closely related to the continuous chain of thought approach explored in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, in the sense that it is an intervention to the trained model to add additional recurrence. To achieve a similar behavior in fixed-depth transformers, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al. (2024)</a></cite> train models on reasoning chains to accept their last hidden state as alternative inputs when computing the next token. Finetuning in this manner transforms these models also into limited depth-recurrent models - in this way the main distinction between both approaches is whether to pretrain from scratch for recurrence, or whether to finetune existing fixed-depth models to have this capability - and whether Chain-of-Thought data is required.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.4 </span>Zero-Shot Self-Speculative Decoding</h3>

<div id="S6.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recurrent-depth models can also inherently generate text more efficiently by using speculative decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib91" title="" class="ltx_ref">Leviathan et al., 2023</a>)</cite> without the need for a separate draft model. With standard transformer models, speculative decoding requires an external draft model, Medusa heads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or early-exit adaptation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib183" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhoushi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib183" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> implement self-speculative decoding simply through layer skipping, but this does not always result in good draft quality.
In comparison, our model can naturally be run with fewer iterations to draft the next <math id="S6.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> tokens in the generated sequence, which can then be verified with any desired number of iterations <math id="S6.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M&gt;N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M&gt;N</annotation></semantics></math> later. This can also be staggered across multiple draft stages, or the draft model can use adaptive compute as in <a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Zero-Shot Adaptive Compute at Test-Time ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>.
Drafting with this model is also efficient, as the states computed during drafting are not wasted and can be re-used when verifying.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlie_highlight_W_155.png" id="S6.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:505/166;" width="505" height="166" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlie_highlight_C_167.png" id="S6.F12.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:505/166;" width="505" height="166" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlie_highlight_I_92.png" id="S6.F12.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:505/166;" width="505" height="166" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 12: </span>Latent Space trajectories for select tokens. We show a small part of these high-dimensional trajectories by visualizing the first 6 PCA directions, computing the PCA over all latent state trajectories of all tokens in a sequence. The color gradient going from dark to bright represents steps in the trajectory. The center of mass is marked in red. While on many tokens, the state simply converges (top row), the model also learns to use orbits (middle row), and “sliders” (bottom row, middle), which we observe being used to represent and handle more advanced concepts, such as arithmetic or complicated deliberation. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>What Mechanisms Emerge at Scale in Recurrent-Depth Models</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, what is the model doing while recurring in latent space? To understand this question better, we analyze the trajectories <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{s}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>r</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{s}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{r}</annotation></semantics></math> of the model on a few qualitative examples. We are especially interested in understanding what patterns emerge, simply by training this model at scale. In comparison to previous work, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2019)</a></cite>, where the training objective directly encodes a prior that pushes trajectories to a fixed point, we only train with our truncated unrolling objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S6.F11" title="In 6.2 Zero-Shot KV-cache Sharing ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> shows the norm distance <math id="S7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||\mathbf{s}_{i}-\mathbf{s}^{*}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||\mathbf{s}_{i}-\mathbf{s}^{*}||</annotation></semantics></math> between each <math id="S7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in a trajectory and an approximate limit point <math id="S7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> computed with 128 iterations. We show the sentence top to bottom and iterations from left to right. We clearly see that convergence behavior depends on context. We see that key parts of the question, and the start of the model response, are “deliberated” much more in latent space. The context dependence can also be seen in the different behavior among the three identical tokens representing each of the three dots. Also note that the distance to <math id="S7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐬</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> does not always decrease monotonically (e.g. for <span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">school</span>); the model may also trace out complicated orbits in its latent trajectory while processing information, even though this is not represented explicitly in our training objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We look at trajectories for select tokens in more detail in <a href="#S6.F12" title="In 6.4 Zero-Shot Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>. We compute a PCA decomposition of latent trajectories over all tokens in a sequence, and then show several individual trajectories projected onto the first six PCA directions. See the appendix for more examples. Many tokens simply converge to a fixed point, such as the token in the top row. Yet, for harder questions, such as in the 2nd row<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          This is the token ”3” in a GSM8k test question that opens with <span id="footnote5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Claire makes a <span id="footnote5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">3</span> egg omelette</span>.</span></span></span>, the state of the token quickly falls into an orbit pattern in all three pairs of PCA directions. The use of multi-dimensional orbits like these could serve a similar purpose to periodic patterns sometimes observed in fixed-depth transformers trained for arithmetic tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib118" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nanda et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, but we find these patterns extend far beyond arithmetic for our model. We often also observe the use of orbits on tokens such as “makes” (see <a href="#A2.F16" title="In Appendix B Latent Space Visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>) or “thinks” that determine the structure of the response.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from orbits, we also observe the model encoding particular key tokens as “sliders”, as seen in the middle of the bottom row in <a href="#S6.F12" title="In 6.4 Zero-Shot Self-Speculative Decoding ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> (which is the token “wrong”, from the same message as already shown in <a href="#S6.F11" title="In 6.2 Zero-Shot KV-cache Sharing ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>). In these motions the trajectory noticeably drifts in a single direction, which the model could use to implement a mechanism to count how many iterations have occurred.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The emergence of structured trajectories in latent space gives us a glimpse into how the model performs its computations. Unlike the discrete sequential chain of reasoning seen in verbalized chain-of-thought approaches, we observe rich geometric patterns including orbits, convergent paths, and drifts - means to organize its computational process spatially. This suggests the model is independently learning to leverage the high-dimensional nature of its latent space to implement reasoning in new ways.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Path Independence.</h4>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We verify that our models maintain path independence, in the sense of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anil et al. (2022)</a></cite>, despite their complex, learned dynamics, which we discussed prior (see also the additional examples in Appendix <a href="#A2.F22" title="In Appendix B Latent Space Visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>). When re-initializing from multiple starting states <math id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{s}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐬</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{s}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, the model moves in similar trajectories, exhibiting consistent behavior. The same orbital patterns, fixed points, or directional drifts emerge regardless of initialization.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Related Work Overview</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The extent to which recurrence is a foundational concept of machine learning is hard to overstate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amari, 1972</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hopfield, 1982</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Braitenberg, 1986</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gers and Schmidhuber, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib151" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sutskever et al., 2008</a>)</cite>. Aside from using recurrence to move along sequences, as in recurrent neural networks, it was understood early to also be the key to adaptive computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib131" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber, 2012</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Graves, 2017</a>)</cite>. For transformers, recurrence was applied in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dehghani et al. (2019)</a></cite>, who highlight the aim of recurrent depth to model <span id="S8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">universal</span>, i.e. Turing-complete, machines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Graves et al., 2014</a>)</cite>. It was used at scale (but with fixed recurrence) in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib87" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lan et al. (2019)</a></cite> and an interesting recent improvement in this line of work are described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib155" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abnar et al. (2023)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathur et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al. (2024)</a></cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib135" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al. (2021b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bear et al. (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">McLeish et al. (2024)</a></cite> show that depth recurrence is advantageous when learning generalizable algorithms when training with randomized unrolling and input injections. Recent work has described depth-recurrent, <span id="S8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">looped</span>, transformers and studied their potential benefits with careful theoretical and small-scale analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Giannou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gatmiry et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib173" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">From another angle, these models can be described as neural networks learning a fixed-point iteration, as studied in <span id="S8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">deep equilibrium</span> models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. They are further related to diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib146" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song and Ermon, 2019</a>)</cite>, especially latent diffusion models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib127" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rombach et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, but we note that language diffusion models are usually run with a per-sequence, instead of a per-token, iteration count <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib90" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. A key difference of our approach to both equilibrium models and diffusion models is in the training objective, where equilibrium methods solve the “direct” problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geiping and Moeller, 2019</a>)</cite>, diffusion models solve a surrogate training objective, and our work suggests that truncated unrolling is a scalable alternative.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">More generally, all architectures that recur in depth can also be understood as directly learning the analog to the gradient of a latent energy-based model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun and Huang, 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib88" title="" class="ltx_ref">LeCun, 2022</a>)</cite>, to an implicitly defined intermediate optimization layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amos and Kolter, 2017</a>)</cite>, or to a Kuramoto layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib113" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miyato et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Analogies to gradient descent at inference time also show the connection to test time adaptation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib150" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, especially test-time adaptation of output states <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Boudiaf et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from full recurrent-depth architectures, there also exist a number of proposals for hybrid architectures, such as models with latent sub-networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib95" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2020a</a>)</cite>, LoRA adapters on top of weight-shared layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bae et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or (dynamic) weight-tying of trained models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hay and Wolf, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in <a href="#S6" title="6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, while we consider the proposed recurrent depth approach to be a very natural way to learn to reason in continuous latent space from the ground up, the works of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng and Durme (2024)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib99" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2024a)</a></cite> discuss how to finetune existing fixed-depth transformers with this capability. These works have a similar aim to ours, enabling reasoning in latent space, but approach this goal from separate directions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p6.1" class="ltx_p">For additional discussions related to the idea of constructing a prior that incentivizes reasoning and algorithm learning at the expense of memorization of simple patterns, we also refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chollet (2019)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib133" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild (2023)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib96" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2020b)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib114" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moulton (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Future Work</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from work extending and analyzing the scaling behaviors of recurrent depth models, there are many questions that remain unanswered. For example, to us, there are potentially a large number of novel post-training schemes that further enhance the capabilities of these models, such as fine-tuning to compress the recurrence or reinforcement learning with data with different hardness levels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib178" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or to internalize reasoning from CoT data into the recurrence <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Another aspect not covered in this work is the relationship to other modern architecture improvements. Efficient sequence mixing operations, especially those that are linear in sequence dimension, such as linear attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Katharopoulos et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib174" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, are limited in the number of comparisons that can be made. However, with recurrent depth, blocks containing linear operators can repeat until all necessary comparisons between sequence elements are computed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib152" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suzgun et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. For simplicity, we also focus on a single recurrence, where prior work has considered multiple successive recurrent stages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib153" title="" class="ltx_ref">Takase and Kiyono, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the proposed architecture is set up to be <span id="S9.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">compute-heavy</span>, with more “materialized” parameters than there are actual parameters. This naturally mirrors mixture-of-expert models (MoE), which are <span id="S9.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">parameter-heavy</span>, using fewer active parameters per forward pass than exist within the model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. We posit that where the recurrent-depth setup excels at learning reasoning patterns, the MoE excels at effectively storing and retrieving complex information. Their complementarity supports the hypothesis that a future architecture would contain both modifications. While in a standard MoE model, each expert can only be activated once per forward pass, or skipped entirely, a recurrent MoE model could also refine its latent state over multiple iterations, potentially routing to the same expert multiple times, before switching to a different one <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib155" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. While MoE models are the currently leading solution to implement this type of “memory” in dense transformers, these considerations also hold for other memory mechanisms suggested for LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib148" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sukhbaatar et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib169" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S10" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">10 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S10.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The models described in this paper are ultimately still a proof-of-concept. We describe how to train a latent recurrent-depth architecture, what parameters we chose, and then trained a single model at scale. Future training runs are likely to train with more optimized learning rate schedules, data mixes and accelerators. Still we observe a number of interesting behaviors emerging naturally from recurrent training. The most important of these is the ability to use latent reasoning to dramatically improve performance on reasoning tasks by expending test-time computation. In addition, we also observe context-dependent convergence speed, path independence, and various zero-shot abilities.
This leads us to believe that latent reasoning is a promising research direction to complement existing approaches for test-time compute scaling. The model we realize is surprisingly powerful given its size and amount of training data, and we are excited about the potential impact of imbuing generative models with the ability to reason in continuous latent space without the need for specialized data at train time or verbalization at inference time.</p>
</div>
</section>
