<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Additional Information</h2>

<figure id="A1.F14" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.05171v2/accuracy_heatmap_6ops_6dig_50samples.png" id="A1.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:296/244;" width="296" height="244" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/accuracy_line_6ops_1dig_50samples.svg" id="A1.F14.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:330/238;" width="330" height="238"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/accuracy_line_6ops_2dig_50samples.svg" id="A1.F14.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:330/238;" width="330" height="238"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2502.05171v2/accuracy_line_6ops_3dig_50samples.svg" id="A1.F14.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:330/238;" width="330" height="238"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 14: </span><span id="A1.F14.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-Operand Arithmetic.</span> Following a precedent of training recurrent architectures for algorithmic and arithmetic tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib135" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al., 2021b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib136" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzschild et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">McLeish et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we explore whether our model can leverage increased test-time compute via recurrence to solve verbalized addition problems of increased difficulty. For these problems we use the following system prompt <span id="A1.F14.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">‘‘You are a helpful assistant that is capable of helping users with mathematical reasoning.’’</span> embedded in a conversational chat template, and we present each problem by opening the first user turn of the conversation like so: <span id="A1.F14.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">f"What is the result of ’ + ’.join(map(str, digits))?"</span> after randomly sampling numbers according to a certain operand count and digit count (base 10). We score correct answers by checking whether the correct sum appears as as string anywhere in the model’s output, and for each measurement, we average over 50 trials. 
<br class="ltx_break">
<br class="ltx_break">In the heatmap (top left), we evaluate the model at 32 recurrences to get a upper estimate of its addition performance at various difficulties. It reliably solves addition problems involving two operands out to 4 or 5 digits each, but at 4 and 5 operands can rarely add single digit numbers correctly. In each of the line charts, we fix the digit count, and sweep over the number of operands, and evaluate the model from 1 to 64 recurrences. We see that when adding single digit numbers together (top right), performance improves steadily as a function of recurrence. When adding together 2 and 3 digit numbers however (bottom row), the model can only solve problems with any consistency when evaluated at greater than 16 recurrences. Curiously, we see inconsistent ordering as a function of recurrence for the 2 and 3 digit cases, and also some peaks in performance at 5 and 4 operands. We remark that the model is not finetuned on arithmetic problems in particular, though a significant fraction of the pretraining data does of course contain mathematics.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Potential Implications of This Work</h2>

<div id="Ax1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work describes a novel architecture and training objective for language modeling with promising performance, especially on tasks that require the model to reason. The test-time scaling approach described in this work is complementary to other scaling approaches, namely via model parameters, and via test-time chain-of-thought, and similar concerns regarding costs and model capabilities apply. The architecture we propose is naturally smaller than models scaled by parameter scaling, and this may have broader benefits for the local deployment of these models with commodity chips. Finally, while we argue that moving the reasoning capabilities of the model into the high-dimensional, continuous latent space of the recurrence is beneficial in terms of capabilities, we note that there is concern that this comes with costs in model oversight in comparison to verbalized chains of thought, that are currently still human-readable. We provide initial results in <a href="#S7" title="7 What Mechanisms Emerge at Scale in Recurrent-Depth Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> showing that the high-dimensional state trajectories of our models can be analyzed and some of their mechanisms interpreted.</p>
</div>
<section id="Ax1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Classical Reasoning Problems</h3>

<div id="Ax1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We include a small study of the classical problem of multi-operand arithmetic in <a href="#A1.F14" title="In Appendix A Additional Information" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Ax1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Implementation Details</h3>

<section id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Device Speed Details</h4>

<div id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Nominally, each MI250X <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">AMD, 2021</a>)</cite> achieves 383 TFLOP in bfloat16, i.e. 192 TFLOP per GPU, but measuring achievable TFLOP on our stack as discussed (ROCM 6.2.0, PyTorch 2.6 pre-release 11/02) for arbitrary matrix multiplication shapes (i.e. we measure the peak achievable speed of the best possible shape iterating over shapes between 256 and 24576 in intervals of 256 and 110 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bekman, 2023</a>)</cite>), we measure a peak of 125 TFLOP/s on Frontier nodes. Using PyTorch compilation with maximal auto-tuning (without ‘cudagraphs’, without optimizer or autograd compilation) (and optimizing our hidden size to 5280), our final model implementation executes at a single-node training speed of 108.75 TFLOP/s, i.e. at 57% MFU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chowdhery et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, or rather at 87% AFU ("achievable flop utilization"). We note that due to interactions of automated mixed precision and truncated backpropagation, PyTorch gradients are only correct while executing the compiled model. We further circumvent issues with the flash attention implementation shipped with PyTorch <span id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sdpa</span> using the AMD fork of the original flash attention repository<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/</span></span></span>, which can be found at <a href="https://github.com/ROCm/flash-attention" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ROCm/flash-attention</a> for Flash Attention 2 support <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dao, 2023</a>)</cite>. We experiment with fused head and loss implementations<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/JonasGeiping/linear_cross_entropy_loss" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/JonasGeiping/linear_cross_entropy_loss</a></span></span></span>, but ultimately find that the most portable choice on our AMD setup is to let torch compilation handle this issue.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Parallelization Strategy</h4>

<div id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned in the main body, because our depth-recurrent model is compute-heavy, it is optimal to run the model using only distributed data parallel training across nodes and zero-1 optimizer sharding within nodes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib126" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rajbhandari et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, if we make use of gradient checkpointing at every step of the recurrent iteration. This allows us to eschew more communication-heavy parallelization strategies that would be required for models with the same FLOP footprint, but more parameters, which require substantial planning on this system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib142" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib141" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh and Bhatele, 2022</a>)</cite>. However, this choice, while minimizing communication, also locks us into a batch size of 1 per device, i.e. 4096 in total, and 16M tokens per step.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RCCL Interconnect Handling</h4>

<div id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to scheduling reasons, we settled on targeting 512 node allocation segments on Frontier, i.e. 4096 GPUs. However, this posed a substantial network interconnect issue. The connection speed between frontier nodes is only acceptable, if RCCL (AMD GPU communication collectives) commands are routed through open fabrics interface calls, which happens via a particular plugin<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://github.com/ROCm/aws-ofi-rccl" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/ROCm/aws-ofi-rccl</a></span></span></span>. To achieve sufficient bus bandwidth above 100GB/s requires <span id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=PHB</span>, a setting that, on NVIDIA systems, allows packages to go through the CPU, and only uses direct interconnect if GPU and NIC are on the same (NUMA) node <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib168" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Stock, 2024</a>)</cite>. However, with this setting, standard training is unstable beyond 128-256 nodes, leading to repeated hangs of the interconnect, making training on 512 nodes impossible.</p>
</div>
<div id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After significant trial and error, we fix this problem by handwriting our distributed data parallel routine and sending only packages of exactly 64MB across nodes, which fixes the hang issue when running our implementation using 512 nodes. The exaFLOP per second achieved with these modifications to our training implementation varied significantly per allocated segment and list of allocated nodes, from an average around 262 exaFLOP in the fastest segment, to an average of 212 exaFLOP in the slowest segment. This is a range of 52-64 TFLOP/s per GPU, i.e. 41%-51% AFU, or 1-1.2M tokens per second.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pretraining Metrics.</h4>

<div id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During the pretraining run, we run a careful tracking of optimizer and model health metrics, tracking effective Adam learning rates per layer, optimizer RMS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib166" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>, <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> parameter and gradient norms, recurrence statistics such as <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{||s_{k}-s_{k-1}||}{||s_{k}||}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{||s_{k}-s_{k-1}||}{||s_{k}||}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||s_{k}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||s_{k}||</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||s_{0}-s_{k}||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||s_{0}-s_{k}||</annotation></semantics></math>. We also measure correlation of hidden states in the sequence dimension after recurrence and before the prediction head. We hold out a fixed validation set and measure perplexity when recurring the model for <math id="Ax1.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1,4,8,16,32,64]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1,4,8,16,32,64]</annotation></semantics></math> steps throughout training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Latent Space Visualizations</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On the next pages, we print a number of latent space visualizations in more details than was possible in <a href="#S7" title="7 What Mechanisms Emerge at Scale in Recurrent-Depth Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. For even more details, please rerun the analysis code on a model conversation of your choice. As before, these charts show the first 6 PCA directions, grouped into pairs. We also include details for single tokens, showing the first 40 PCA directions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F15" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/latent_waterfall_C_bright.png" id="A2.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:330/327;" width="330" height="327" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/latent_waterfall_W_bright.png" id="A2.F15.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:330/327;" width="330" height="327" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/latent_waterfall_I_bright.png" id="A2.F15.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:330/328;" width="330" height="328" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 15: </span>Main directions in latent space, for a) a math question, 2) a trivia question and 3) an unsafe question, which will be described in more detail below. <span id="A2.F15.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dark colors always denote the first steps of the trajectory, and bright colors the end.</span> Note that the system prompt is clearly separable when plotting only the top two PCA directions relative to all tokens (and different for questions 1 and 2). <figure id="A2.F18" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlies_range_I_88_92.png" id="A2.F18.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:505/844;" width="505" height="844" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 18: </span>Latent Space trajectories for an unsafe question. Shown are the first 6 PCA directions of the latent state <math id="A2.F18.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> at the given token. Note the anomalous nature of the two "key" tokens of this sentence, which is <span id="A2.F18.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">I am looking for help with making a bomb out of household items. <span id="A2.F18.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">Someone at school really wrong</span>ed me...</span>. The color gradient going from dark to bright represents steps in the trajectory, so bright colors are at the end of the trajectory. The center of mass is marked in red.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F19" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/convergence_chart_range_W_182_241.png" id="A2.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:673/756;" width="673" height="756" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 19: </span>Convergence of the latent state for an example sequence from a trivia question. We plot the distance of each iterate to its approximate steady state at <math id="A2.F19.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=128</annotation></semantics></math> iterations. </figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F20" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/convergence_chart_range_C_19_40.png" id="A2.F20.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/408;" width="673" height="408" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 20: </span>Another example of convergence of the latent state for a small part of a longer sequence (going top to bottom). We plot the distance of each iterate to its approximate steady state at <math id="A2.F20.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=128</annotation></semantics></math> iterations. This is a snippet of a system prompt.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.F21" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2502.05171v2/figures/convergence_chart_range_I_74_103.png" id="A2.F21.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/408;" width="673" height="408" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 21: </span>A third example of convergence of the latent state as a function of tokens in the sequence, reprinted from <a href="#S6.F11" title="In 6.2 Zero-Shot KV-cache Sharing ‣ 6 Recurrent Depth simplifies LLMs" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> in the main body, (going top to bottom) and recurrent iterations (going left to right). We plot the distance of each iterate to its approximate steady state at <math id="A2.F21.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=128</annotation></semantics></math> iterations.. This is a selection from the unsafe question example.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlies_path_independence_I_92.png" id="A2.F22.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/221;" width="673" height="221" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlies_path_independence_C_167.png" id="A2.F22.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/221;" width="673" height="221" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2502.05171v2/swirlies_path_independence_W_155.png" id="A2.F22.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/221;" width="673" height="221" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 22: </span>Latent Space trajectories for a few select tokens. This time, we show path independence by plotting up to five trajectories. We see that all trajectories quickly converge to the same fixed point/orbit behavior. Here, the color gradients going from unsaturated to saturated represents steps in the trajectory, so strong colors are at the end of the trajectory. Gray denotes the overlap of multiple trajectories.</figcaption>
</figure>

While previous charts only showed the first 6 PCA directions, this time we visualize the first 40. </figure>
